journal_name: IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework called Distributed Consensus through Temporal Logic (DCTL) that fundamentally reimagines fault-tolerant agreement protocols in large-scale distributed systems. Traditional Byzantine fault tolerance mechanisms rely on synchronous assumptions or probabilistic guarantees, which limit their applicability in modern cloud computing and data center environments. We propose a formal model that decomposes consensus into temporal proof obligations verified through recursive verification rounds. Our theoretical analysis establishes that DCTL achieves deterministic consensus under partial synchrony with communication complexity O(n log n), where n represents the number of nodes, representing a polynomial reduction compared to classical solutions. We further prove that the framework naturally extends to handle selfish and rational adversaries in addition to Byzantine failures, enabling a unified treatment of security and incentive compatibility. The analysis introduces the concept of temporal certificate chains that amortize verification costs across multiple consensus instances. We provide rigorous correctness proofs using refinement mappings and demonstrate that the framework remains robust under adversarial network scheduling. This work opens new theoretical directions for combining formal methods with distributed computing, potentially impacting the design of next-generation high-performance computing systems and blockchain protocols.

This paper presents rigorous theoretical analysis that substantially improves upon existing approximation algorithms for the NP-hard problem of deadline-constrained task scheduling in heterogeneous distributed computing environments. Prior work established that list scheduling heuristics achieve approximation ratios of (2 - 1/m) for m heterogeneous machines, while more sophisticated algorithms using linear programming relaxation attain ratios approaching 1.58 under restrictive assumptions about task parallelism. We develop a novel primal-dual scheduling framework that combines adaptive task clustering with deferred decision-making to achieve a provable approximation ratio of 1.45 for arbitrary task parallelism levels. Our analysis introduces the concept of parallelism-aware duality gaps that capture the structural tension between task heterogeneity and machine diversity. We prove that the algorithm's performance guarantee gracefully degrades with reduced machine pools while maintaining competitive ratios better than 1.5 even when machine availability drops to 20% of nominal capacity. Furthermore, we establish improved bounds for the special case of bag-of-tasks workloads commonly appearing in big data processing applications on Spark and MapReduce platforms. Complexity analysis demonstrates that our algorithm achieves near-linear time complexity O(mn log(n)), making it suitable for dynamic resource management in cloud computing scenarios. Simulation results on synthetic and trace-driven workloads validate the theoretical bounds.

We present Gaia, a decentralized cloud computing platform that fundamentally reconceptualizes resource management in geo-distributed data centers through blockchain-based smart contracts. Existing cloud platforms rely on centralized resource managers that create single points of failure and introduce substantial coordination overhead, particularly problematic for latency-sensitive applications requiring geographic distribution. Gaia replaces this centralized architecture with a distributed ledger that records resource allocations, enables verifiable pricing mechanisms, and enforces Service Level Agreements through executable contract logic. The system introduces a novel consensus mechanism called Proof of Computational Contribution that validates resource consumption claims without requiring energy-intensive cryptographic puzzles. We implement Gaia across 12 geographically distributed nodes spanning three continents and evaluate its performance using microbenchmarks, macrobenchmarks based on Google cluster traces, and real applications including machine learning inference and stream processing workloads. Results demonstrate that Gaia achieves transaction throughput exceeding 50,000 operations per second while maintaining sub-second finality for resource allocation decisions. The platform supports pluggable scheduling policies that can encode complex organizational requirements while preserving the transparency benefits of distributed ledgers. We provide detailed analysis of security properties, demonstrating resistance to Sybil attacks through identity verification integrated with the resource provisioning workflow.

This paper presents StreamFlow, an improved stream processing system that significantly advances the state-of-the-art in elastic resource management for big data applications. While existing systems like Apache Flink and Spark Streaming provide basic elasticity mechanisms, they suffer from significant reconfiguration overhead and poor performance during dynamic scaling events due to coarse-grained operator migration. StreamFlow introduces a fine-grained dataflow migration approach that allows operators to be decomposed into sub-operator fragments that can migrate independently based on real-time load predictions. The system incorporates a machine learning-based predictor that anticipates workload changes 30-60 seconds ahead using historical pattern analysis, enabling proactive scaling that eliminates reactive thrashing. We implement StreamFlow as an extension to Apache Spark and evaluate it using standard benchmarks including WordCount, Grep, and Join operations, as well as real-world streaming workloads from financial transaction processing and IoT sensor data analysis. Compared to Spark Streaming's default elasticity mechanisms, StreamFlow reduces latency degradation during scaling events by 73% while improving overall throughput by 41%. The system maintains exactly-once processing semantics throughout migrations and demonstrates graceful degradation under fault injection. We provide detailed performance analysis demonstrating that the prediction overhead remains below 5% of total processing capacity, ensuring that proactive optimization does not consume excessive resources.
